A suspension bridge is one of the most elegant and efficient structures in civil engineering, capable of spanning vast distances with minimal material usage. Its ability to carry heavy loads relies on a sophisticated interplay of tension and compression forces, distributed among several key components: the main cables, the towers, the deck, and the anchorages.

The primary load-bearing elements are the main cables, which are typically made of high-strength steel wire. These cables are draped over the tops of two massive towers and are anchored firmly into concrete blocks or bedrock at each end of the bridge. The cables are not simply hung loosely; they are pre-tensioned to create a catenary curve, which is the natural shape a flexible cable takes under its own weight. This pre-tensioning is crucial because it allows the cables to support the weight of the bridge deck and any traffic on it.

When a vehicle or pedestrian steps onto the deck, their weight is transferred to the deck itself. The deck is not a rigid beam that resists bending; instead, it is suspended from the main cables by vertical suspender cables (or hangers).
